article_title: Trump imposes sweeping new tariffs on Chinese goods in escalating trade war
article_summary: President Trump signed an executive order imposing new tariffs on Chinese imports, escalating the ongoing trade dispute.
article_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order imposing sweeping new tariffs on Chinese goods, dramatically escalating a trade war that has unsettled global markets and strained diplomatic relations between the world's two largest economies.

The new measures, which Trump described as necessary to protect American manufacturers and workers, will impose a 25 percent tariff on a broad range of consumer electronics, machinery, and industrial components imported from China. The tariffs are set to take effect within 30 days, giving businesses limited time to adjust supply chains.

"China has been taking advantage of the United States for decades," Trump told reporters at the White House. "This is going to change. American workers and American companies will no longer be treated unfairly."

Beijing swiftly condemned the announcement. China's Ministry of Commerce said in a statement that it "firmly opposes" the tariffs and warned that China would take "countermeasures" to protect its economic interests. Chinese officials did not specify what those measures might entail, but analysts said retaliatory tariffs on American agricultural exports and technology companies were possible.

The announcement sent shockwaves through financial markets. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 400 points in early trading, while shares of major technology companies with significant exposure to Chinese manufacturing, including Apple, Dell, and HP, dropped sharply. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note also fell as investors sought safe-haven assets.

Economists offered mixed assessments of the policy. Supporters argued that the tariffs would help reduce the trade deficit with China, which reached a record 380 billion dollars last year, and incentivize the return of manufacturing jobs to the United States. Critics warned that the measures would raise consumer prices, disrupt global supply chains, and invite retaliation that could harm American exporters, particularly farmers.

"Every tariff is ultimately a tax on the American consumer," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "These measures may score political points, but they will raise prices on everyday goods and could tip a fragile global economy toward recession."

The Trump administration has argued that previous administrations were too soft on China and that only firm action could force Beijing to change what it calls unfair trade practices, including the forced transfer of American technology, currency manipulation, and state subsidies to domestic industries.

In Congress, reaction split largely along partisan lines. Republican leaders praised the measure as long overdue, while Democratic lawmakers expressed concern about the potential impact on consumers and trading relationships.

Senator Maria Cantwell, Democrat of Washington, warned that the tariffs could damage the aviation and agriculture sectors, which depend heavily on exports to China. "We need a strategy, not a shock to the system," she said.

Some Republican senators from farm states also expressed reservations, noting that Chinese retaliatory tariffs on soybeans and pork during a previous trade dispute in 2018 had inflicted serious pain on agricultural communities.

The new tariffs come as part of a broader reassessment of United States trade policy under Trump, who has also imposed or threatened tariffs on goods from Canada, Mexico, and the European Union. Critics argue that the approach is destabilizing the rules-based international trading system built over decades.

Chinese state media responded to Monday's announcement with editorials accusing the United States of economic bullying and calling on other countries to unite in opposition to what they called unilateral coercion.

Trade economists said the full impact of the measures would take months to become clear, as businesses and governments work out how to respond.
